title: A Queue Without a Lock, and What Acquire and Release Actually Mean

questions.question: Why is a mutex the wrong tool between a sensor thread and a control loop with a deadline?
options: Because mutexes require dynamic allocation
Mutexes cannot be used between two threads
A mutex copies the data twice
How long you wait depends on what the holder is doing, which is unbounded
questions.explanation: The holder might be descheduled halfway through while still holding it. A deadline cares about the worst case, and a mutex cannot promise one.

questions.question: Why does restricting the queue to one producer and one consumer make it simple?
options: Each index is written by exactly one thread, so no index is ever contended
It removes the need for atomics entirely
It halves the memory needed
It allows the compiler to inline everything
questions.explanation: That restriction is the design rather than a compromise, and it is also the shape robotics needs: one sensor thread producing, one control thread consuming.

questions.question: Why keep one slot of the buffer permanently empty?
options: To leave room for the largest reading
To make the buffer cache aligned
Because the modulus requires an odd size
So that head equal to tail means empty unambiguously, with no extra shared state
questions.explanation: The alternative is a separate count, which is another shared variable and therefore another ordering problem. One wasted element is cheaper.

questions.question: What does storing the index with release ordering guarantee?
options: That the store happens immediately
Everything written before it is visible to a thread that acquires that same variable
That no other thread writes the index at the same time
That the store itself is not torn
questions.explanation: The atomic alone only protects the index. Release and acquire are what carry the reading it points at across to the other thread.

questions.question: Measured on a real machine, how did the lock free queue compare with a mutex queue?
options: Identical in every measure
Worse in the median but better in the worst case
Median about three times better and the 99th percentile about nine times, with the worst case not reliably better
Better by about ninety times in every measure
questions.explanation: The worst case is dominated by the operating system descheduling the thread, which no data structure can prevent. The common claim of bounded latency did not survive measurement.

questions.question: What does lock free actually promise?
options: A bounded worst case latency
That every operation is wait free
No thread is blocked because another thread holding a lock was descheduled
That the structure is faster in every case
questions.explanation: It is a smaller claim than usually made for it. A real bound needs a kernel that will not deschedule the thread arbitrarily, which is a later lesson.
